narrative:
The model estimates a 37% chance that you will not pass your final year. That does not mean failure is certain, but it is a substantial risk, so the school is placing you in remedial courses as a required support step. Your sex, age, and health did not drive this decision.

The strongest reason the prediction leaned toward failing was your previous class failure: you have one past failure, while students who passed had none on average. That prior setback is the main risk signal. Two other important factors worked in your favor. Your weekly study time of five to ten hours pushed toward passing and is stronger than the typical passing student, most of whom study only two to five hours. Your plan to continue to higher education also pushed toward passing and matches the aspiration of all students who passed. These strengths lower the estimated risk, but they do not fully offset the earlier failure.

To improve your chances, treat the remedial courses as targeted help rather than punishment. Use them to repair the specific gaps behind your past failure, keep your current study routine, and ask teachers for feedback on where marks are being lost. Since you are not currently receiving school, family, or paid educational support, consider requesting tutoring or regular check-ins. Maintain attendance—your four absences are close to average—and focus extra effort on the subject most connected to the previous failure.
